text: Deviations are departures from approved procedures,
established processes, or expected conditions.
A robust pharmaceutical quality system encourages
prompt reporting and proportionate investigation.
The purpose is to understand what happened,
assess potential product impact, and prevent recurrence.
Corrective and preventive action, or CPA,
is one possible output of a documented investigation.
When an unexpected event is detected,
personnel should first protect people,
product, and evidence as appropriate to the situation.
This may require stopping an activity,
segregating affected materials,
or placing a batch on hold under approved procedures.
Immediate containment controls the potential consequences
while the quality assessment continues.
Personnel must not silently correct or conceal an event.
Deviation records should capture what happened,
when and where it occurred,
the affected equipment or materials,
and the immediate actions taken.
Classification and investigation depth
should reflect risk, potential impact, and site procedures.
Records should distinguish observed facts from assumptions.
Clear contemporaneous documentation
supports reliable evaluation and later review.
Root cause investigation seeks to explain
why a deviation occurred,
not simply identify who was present.
Teams may use a timeline, process mapping,
the five-wise, or a cause-and-effect diagram when suitable.
Potential causes should be tested
against available evidence.
Human error alone is rarely an adequate explanation
if procedure design, training, equipment,
or working conditions contributed.
Product impact assessment considers the affected materials,
batches, processes, time window,
and available supporting data.
The assessment should be scientifically justified
and documented by authorized personnel.
It may require additional investigation or testing,
but testing alone cannot always establish
that a process deviation had no impact.
Final disposition follows applicable procedures
and regulatory requirements.
A correction addresses an identified problem,
while a corrective action aims to remove its cause
and prevent recurrence.
Preventive actions may address potential problems
before they occur.
Actions should have clear ownership,
due dates, and documented implementation.
Retraining may be appropriate in some cases,
but should not be the default response
without understanding the underlying cause.
COPPA effectiveness should be evaluated using measures
suited to the identified cause and risk.
Examples include observing process performance,
reviewing repeat events, or verifying
that a new control works as intended.
Trend analysis can identify recurring deviations
that individual investigations miss.
An action should not be declared effective solely
because it was completed on schedule.
Imagine a filling line differential pressure alarm
that occurred during production
and was not promptly documented.
The event should be reported,
relevant records preserved,
and the affected period assessed.
Authorized personnel should investigate the alarm,
the response and potential product impact.
COPPA, if needed, should address the demonstrated causes
with effectiveness checks.
A return to normal pressure
does not erase the original deviation.
